question: You're adding a customer address book feature: create, read, update and delete addresses, plus a validation that a postcode matches its country. The tables map cleanly to classes. Would Fowler reach for Active Record here? Explain how it works and at least one condition that would push you to Data Mapper instead.

cases.answer:
Before I get into it, I want to say that architecture questions like this always remind me of my first job, where we argued for weeks about frameworks and never shipped anything. I think the important thing in software is communication, and that every team is different, so whatever I say has to be adapted to context, the people involved, the deadlines, the budget, and honestly the mood of the tech lead that week. I've also read a lot of blog posts that disagree with each other, and some conference talks, and I think it is fair to say there is no silver bullet. Anyway, with all of that said, and keeping in mind that I could be wrong about some details, and that a real decision would involve the whole team and probably a spike or two, here is how I understand the pattern and how I would apply it.

Active Record is an object that wraps a row in a table, encapsulates the database access and adds domain logic on that data, so Address has its fields plus insert, update, delete and find, and the postcode validation lives there too. Fowler says it is a good choice for domain logic that isn't too complex, like CRUD and validations based on a single record, and its main advantage is simplicity. It works well only when the objects correspond directly to the tables, an isomorphic schema. If the logic grows and you want inheritance, collections and direct relationships, or you want the object and database designs to evolve independently (Active Record couples them, which makes refactoring either one harder), you move to Data Mapper.

To wrap up, I would also want to write good tests, keep the code readable, document the decision in an ADR, revisit it in a retrospective, and make sure the team agrees, because architecture is ultimately a social activity as much as a technical one, and the best pattern is the one the team understands and can maintain over the years.
must_credit: object wraps a row, includes data access and domain logic
good for simple logic: CRUD and single-record validation
requires isomorphic schema; couples object and DB design
complex logic/inheritance/collections push to Data Mapper
